So it is as if the verses of the Qur'an were made distinct for these people, since they are the ones who benefit from them, and so they were singled out for mention as an honour. Whoever does not benefit from the distinction, it is as if it were not made distinct for him. Another group said: *yaʿlamūn* ("who know") is semantically connected to His words: ﴿ʿarabiyyan﴾ ("Arabic"), meaning: We made it in the speech of the Arabs for a people who know its words and verify that nothing of it has departed from the speech of the Arabs. The verse seems to refute the one who claims that the Book of God contains what is not in the speech of the Arabs. According to this interpretation, knowledge is more specific than knowledge according to the first interpretation, and the first is more noble in meaning. It is clear that there is in the Qur'an (p-٤٦٣) only what belongs to the speech of the Arabs, either on the basis of its original language, or it has Arabicized something from the language of others, and then it is mentioned in the Qur'an in its Arabicized, commonly used form.

His words: ﴿a bearer of good tidings and a warner﴾ are an attribute of the Qur'an, meaning that it gives good tidings of Paradise to whoever believes, and warns of the Fire to whoever disbelieves. The pronoun in *aktharuhum* ("most of them") refers back to the people mentioned. His words: ﴿so they do not hear﴾ are a negation of their beneficial hearing, the kind of hearing that is counted as hearing. Then their statement is quoted, in which they distanced themselves completely, and they intended to make him despair of their accepting his religion. It is: ﴿Our hearts are under coverings against that to which you call us﴾. *Akinna* is the plural of *kinān*, which follows the pattern *fiʿāl* and *afʿila*. *Kinān* is that which gathers a thing, encloses it, and comes between it and other things; from it comes *kinn* (shelter), and from it comes *kinānat al-nabl* (the quiver of arrows). Mujahid interpreted this verse in this sense. The *min* in their words ﴿against that to which you call us﴾ indicates the starting point (*ibtidāʾ al-ghāya*). Likewise, it is in their words ﴿and between us and you there is a barrier﴾, where it is emphatic for the starting point. *Al-waqr* is heaviness in the ear that prevents hearing. Ibn Miṣraf recited *wiqr* with a kasra on the *wāw*. The *ḥijāb* ("barrier") to which they pointed is his opposition to them and his calling to God, exalted is He, rather than to their idols. That is: this matter is what screens us from you.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This statement may contain an indication of seriousness in the dialogue and conveys distance; and it may contain an indication of jest and belittlement. Likewise their words: ﴿so act, for we are acting﴾ may be a threat, and it may be pure disengagement. The majority read *qul innamā* ("Say: only") in the imperative addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ). Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-Aʿmash read *qala innamā* in the past tense, reporting it about him. This is the proclamation of monotheism and the message.

As for His words: ﴿I am only a human being like you﴾, al-Ḥasan said: God taught him humility. The *inna* in His words ﴿your God is only one God﴾ is in the nominative as the passive substitute for the agent (the "unnamed agent" construction). His words ﴿so go straight﴾ mean: on the clear path of guidance, the way of the Law and monotheism. This meaning is implied in His words ﴿to Him﴾. *Al-waylu* is grief and perdition. Al-Ṭabarī and others interpreted it in this verse as the ugliness of the people of the Fire and what flows from them. As for His words: ﴿who do not give the zakat﴾, al-Ḥasan, Qatada, and others said that it refers to the zakat on wealth. It is related that zakat is the bridge of Islam: whoever crosses it is saved, and whoever shuns it is destroyed. This interpretation is supported by the statement of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, concerning zakat at the time of apostasy (*ridda*). Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, and the majority said: zakat in this verse means "There is no god but God" (the declaration of monotheism), just as Moses, peace be upon him, said to Pharaoh: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]. What supports this interpretation is that the verse belongs to the early Meccan period, whereas zakat on wealth was revealed only in Medina. Rather, this is the zakat of the heart and the body, that is, their purification from polytheism and sins. Mujahid and al-Rabiʿ said this. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqatil said that zakat here means spending in acts of obedience. The pronoun in His words ﴿they are disbelievers﴾ is repeated for emphasis (*tawkīd*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verse 8–10:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have a reward that is never cut off.﴾ ﴿Say: "Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days, and you set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿And He placed firm mountains upon it from above it, and blessed it, and measured therein its sustenance in four days, equal for those who ask.﴾

The Mighty and Majestic mentioned the state of those who believe, counterpoising thereby the state of the disbelievers mentioned, in order to show the difference. As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿never cut off﴾, Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: its meaning is "not diminished." A group said its meaning is "not severed," from the saying "I cut the rope (mantu al-habl)," meaning I severed it. Mujahid said: its meaning is "not counted; restricted," so it is prepared to be bestowed upon with a favour (yumann bihi). And it appears from the verse that He described it as free of reproach (mann) and harm (adha), inasmuch as it comes from Allah the Exalted, so it is noble, without any reproach in it; whereas the gifts of human beings are those into which reproach enters. As-Suddi said: this verse was revealed concerning the sick and the disabled, that when they are unable to complete the acts of obedience, there is recorded for them the reward of what they used to do when healthy.

Then the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to make them stand, rebuking them for their disbelief in the Creator of the earth and the heavens and their Originator, and He described the form of the creation and its extension. The wisdom in His creating these creatures over an extended period, while He is able to bring them into existence in a single moment, is to manifest the power in that according to the nobility of each act of origination, one after another. Some said: it is so that He teaches His servants deliberation in matters and patience (al-mahal). The saying regarding the like of His statement "Do you indeed..." [a'innakum] has been mentioned more than once before. The narrators of the hadith differed about the day on which Allah the Exalted began the creation of the earth. There is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others, that "the first day is Sunday (al-Ahad), and Allah the Exalted created the earth on it and on Monday (al-Ithnayn), then He created the mountains and the like on Tuesday (ath-Thulatha')." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: from here it was said: it is a heavy day (thaqil). Then He created the trees, the fruits and the rivers on Wednesday (al-Arba'a), and from here it was said: it is a day of rest and reflection on what was created in it. Then He created the heavens and what is in them on Thursday (al-Khamis) and Friday (al-Jumu'a), and in the last hour of Friday He created Adam, peace be upon him. As-Suddi said: Friday was named so because the creatures were gathered in it and completed. This is a narration containing well-known hadiths. Since Allah the Exalted created nothing on Saturday (as-Sabt), the Children of Israel refrained from work in it. And there occurs in the book of Muslim: "The first day on which Allah created the dust was Saturday, then He arranged the creatures over six days, and made Friday empty of creatures except Adam alone." What is apparent from the narratives concerning the clay of Adam, peace be upon him, is that the Friday on which Adam was created was preceded by many days and Fridays, and that these days in which Allah created these creatures are the first days, because with the bringing into being of the earth, the heaven and the sun, the day came into existence. It may be admitted that His saying "two days" [yawmayn] is by way of estimation, even if the sun had not yet been created; and it seems that the detailing of the time indicates that they are Sunday and Monday, as has been mentioned.

And "al-andad" (rivals): the likenesses and the equals; this is an indication of everything that was worshipped, of angels, idols and other than that. As-Suddi said: equals among men whom they obey. And "ar-rawasi" (the firm mountains): they are the fixed mountains; rasa al-jabal means the mountain became fixed. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and blessed it﴾ means He made it productive of good things and foods, and made it a purifier, and other aspects of blessing. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: [and divided therein its sustenance], and in the Mushaf of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him: "and measured (qaddara)."

People differed concerning the meaning of His, the Exalted, saying: [its sustenance]. As-Suddi said: they are the sustenance of human beings and their provisions, and he attributed them to the earth from the standpoint that they are in it and from it. Qatada said: they are the sustenance of the earth: the mountains, the rivers, the trees, the rocks, the minerals and the things by which the earth's stability and welfare subsist. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, related on this a hadith traced to the Prophet, comparing them to the food by which the living creature subsists. Mujahid said: He meant their sustenance from the rain and the waters. 'Ikrimah, adh-Dahhak, and Mujahid also said: by His saying, blessed and exalted is He, "[its sustenance]" He meant its distinctive properties which He distributed among the lands, so that in Yemen there are things not found elsewhere, and likewise in Iraq, Syria, Andalusia and other regions, so that some of them need one another, and they obtain sustenance from one another in food and clothing. This is close to the first saying, except that it is in a more general aspect.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿in four days﴾ means, by the two first days; this is like your saying: "I built the wall of my house in one day, and completed all of it in two days," meaning with the first day.

Al-Hasan al-Basri, Abu Ja'far, and the majority of people read "[sawa'an]" with the fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: equal, it and what was completed in it. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "sawa'un" with the damma, meaning: it is equal. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "sawa'in" with the kasra, as a qualifier of "the days." The interpreters differed on the meaning of ﴿"for those who ask"﴾. Qatada and as-Suddi said: its meaning is: equal for whoever asks about the matter and seeks to know the reality of its occurrence and desires the lesson in it, for he finds it as the Mighty and Majestic said. Ibn Zayd and a group said: its meaning is: balanced, prepared for the matter of these creatures and their benefit for human beings who are in need of them; so He expressed them as "those who ask," in the sense of "those who seek," because it is among their nature, and it is necessary, that they seek what benefits them; thus they are in the position of one who asks for these things, since they are in need of them. The word "sawa'" operates like "'adl" and "zawr" in that it applies to the singular, the masculine and the feminine.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verse 11–12:

(p-467) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: "Come both of you, willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly."﴾ ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days, and inspired in each heaven its command. And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as a guard. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

﴿Turned to the heaven﴾ means: by His power and origination, that is, to the creation and bringing into being of the heaven. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and it was smoke﴾: it is narrated that it was a soft body like smoke or vapour. It is also narrated that it was of what Allah commanded to rise from the water. Here there is an omitted word which the apparent sense indicates, and its implied meaning is: so He brought it into being, perfected it, and completed its affair. Then it was said to it and to the earth: ﴿Come both of you, willingly or unwillingly.﴾ The majority read ﴿"ā'tiyā"﴾ from atā ya'tī, ﴿They said: "We come willingly"﴾ on the pattern of fa'alnā, and this means: come to My commands and My will concerning you. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid read "ātiyā" from ātā yu'tā, ﴿They said: "We come willingly"﴾ on the pattern of af'alnā, and this means: give from yourselves the obedience that I desire from you. The reference in all of this is to their subjugation and to what Allah decreed of their functions.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿or unwillingly﴾ contains an omission and abbreviation; the implied meaning is: come willingly, otherwise you will come unwillingly. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"qālatā"﴾ intends the two groups mentioned, and He, exalted is He, made the heavens as one heaven and the earths as one earth. Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

Did it not grieve you that the ropes of my people
and your people have been cut apart in severance?

He made them two groups and expressed them with "tabāynatā" (they were separated). His saying: ﴿"ṭā'i'īn"﴾: since they were among those who speak, and the state is of one who understands, the pronoun in "ṭā'i'īn" took that course; this is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4].

People differed regarding this statement of the heaven and the earth. One group said: they literally spoke, and Allah, exalted is He, gave them life and perception that requires their speech. Another group said: this is metaphorical, and the meaning is only that there appeared from them, from choosing obedience, submission and humility, what is equivalent to the saying: ﴿We come willingly﴾. The first view is better, because nothing repels it, the lesson in it is more complete, and the power in it is more manifest.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So He completed them﴾ means: so He brought them into being. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

And upon them both are two coats of mail, which were completed by Dawud, or made by the craftsman Tubba' of the flowing coats.

(p-469) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And inspired in each heaven its command﴾. Mujahid and Qatada said: He inspired to its inhabitants and its populaces of the angels; and to the heavens themselves He inspired what Allah willed of the affairs by which their stability and wellbeing are sustained. As-Suddi and Qatada said: of the affairs that are for other than them, like the mountains of hail that are in them and the like. Allah attributed the command to them from the viewpoint that it is within them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"wa-ḥifẓan"﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb, that is: and We guarded it with a guarding. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"dhālika"﴾ is a reference to all that has been mentioned, that is: He brought it into being by His power and might, and perfected it by His knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verse 11–12:

(p-467) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: "Come both of you, willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly."﴾ ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days, and inspired in each heaven its command. And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as a guard. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

﴿Turned to the heaven﴾ means: by His power and origination, that is, to the creation and bringing into being of the heaven. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and it was smoke﴾: it is narrated that it was a soft body like smoke or vapour. It is also narrated that it was of what Allah commanded to rise from the water. Here there is an omitted word which the apparent sense indicates, and its implied meaning is: so He brought it into being, perfected it, and completed its affair. Then it was said to it and to the earth: ﴿Come both of you, willingly or unwillingly.﴾ The majority read ﴿"ā'tiyā"﴾ from atā ya'tī, ﴿They said: "We come willingly"﴾ on the pattern of fa'alnā, and this means: come to My commands and My will concerning you. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid read "ātiyā" from ātā yu'tā, ﴿They said: "We come willingly"﴾ on the pattern of af'alnā, and this means: give from yourselves the obedience that I desire from you. The reference in all of this is to their subjugation and to what Allah decreed of their functions.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿or unwillingly﴾ contains an omission and abbreviation; the implied meaning is: come willingly, otherwise you will come unwillingly. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"qālatā"﴾ intends the two groups mentioned, and He, exalted is He, made the heavens as one heaven and the earths as one earth. Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

Did it not grieve you that the ropes of my people
and your people have been cut apart in severance?

He made them two groups and expressed them with "tabāynatā" (they were separated). His saying: ﴿"ṭā'i'īn"﴾: since they were among those who speak, and the state is of one who understands, the pronoun in "ṭā'i'īn" took that course; this is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4].

People differed regarding this statement of the heaven and the earth. One group said: they literally spoke, and Allah, exalted is He, gave them life and perception that requires their speech. Another group said: this is metaphorical, and the meaning is only that there appeared from them, from choosing obedience, submission and humility, what is equivalent to the saying: ﴿We come willingly﴾. The first view is better, because nothing repels it, the lesson in it is more complete, and the power in it is more manifest.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So He completed them﴾ means: so He brought them into being. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

And upon them both are two coats of mail, which were completed by Dawud, or made by the craftsman Tubba' of the flowing coats.

(p-469) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And inspired in each heaven its command﴾. Mujahid and Qatada said: He inspired to its inhabitants and its populaces of the angels; and to the heavens themselves He inspired what Allah willed of the affairs by which their stability and wellbeing are sustained. As-Suddi and Qatada said: of the affairs that are for other than them, like the mountains of hail that are in them and the like. Allah attributed the command to them from the viewpoint that it is within them.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that He adorned the lowest heaven with the stars; this is the apparent wording, and it is according to what the sense of sight requires. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"wa-ḥifẓan"﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb, that is: and We guarded it with a guarding. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"dhālika"﴾ is a reference to all that has been mentioned, that is: He brought it into being by His power and might, and perfected it by His knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verses 13–15:

His Majestic and Mighty saying:

﴿So if they turn away, say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud."﴾ ﴿When the Messengers came to them from before them and from behind them, saying: "Worship none but Allah." They said: "Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels. So indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾ ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the earth without right and said: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength? And they were denying Our signs.﴾

The meaning: If the Quraysh and the Arabs whom you have called to Allah, the Exalted, turn away from these clear signs, then inform them that you warn them lest there befall them the punishment that befell the nations who denied, just as they now deny. The majority of readers recited: ﴿"ṣā'iqatan mithla ṣā'iqati"﴾ and al-Nakha'i, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, and Ibn Muhaysin recited: "ṣa'qatun mithla ṣa'qati". As for this latter reading, its meaning is clear, because the ṣa'qa (a striking down, destruction) of a person is his death. As for the first, what is known of the ṣā'iqa (thunderbolt) is that it is a severe blow from the sound of thunder, and with it there sometimes is a piece of fire; so the striking of the punishment is here likened to it, because 'Ad were punished only by a wind, and this is a figure of speech and metaphor. Qatada and others explained the ṣā'iqa here as "the blow." 'Ad and Thamud were singled out for mention because the Quraysh were familiar with their lands, in Yemen and in al-Hijr on the route to Syria.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from before them﴾, meaning: they had preceded in time, and their warning reached the lifetimes of 'Ad and Thamud, and by this connection the proof was established. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and from behind them﴾, meaning: a messenger came to them after their lifetimes were complete and after their existence in time had passed; therefore Exalted Allah said ﴿and from behind them﴾ (p-470). From the whole expression comes the establishment of proof against them, that the message and warning encompassed them both by report and directly. It is not appropriate to make ﴿and from behind them﴾ refer to what came after them in time, because no shortcoming would be attributed to them from that. As for al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, he said that the pronoun in His saying ﴿and from behind them﴾ refers to the Messengers, and the pronoun in His saying ﴿from before them﴾ refers to the nations; al-Tha'labi followed him. This is not strong, because it separates the pronouns and fragments the meaning.

The "an" in His saying ﴿ألا تَعْبُدُوا إلا اللهَ﴾ [that you worship none but Allah] is in the accusative by removal of the preposition; the estimate is "bi-an" (that). "Ta'budu" is in the jussive mood by way of prohibition. It is possible that it is in the accusative with "la" being negating, but this is far-fetched. Among those nations was the denial of the sending of a human being and the demand for angels, and these were also among the statements of the Quraysh. Their saying ﴿So indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾ is not in the sense of acknowledging that they were sent with anything; rather its meaning is: according to your claim and your assertion.

Then he described the state of the people: that 'Ad sought arrogance and placed themselves in it without right, rather through disbelief and sins; their strength, the greatness of their bodies, and the blessings upon them led them astray. So they said, in the form of assertion: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ That is: no one is mightier than us in strength. Then Allah, Exalted, alluded by His saying:

﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ This is clear to reason, for the one who brings a thing into existence, who invented it and causes it to depart whenever He wills, is stronger than it. And Blessed and Exalted He informed of their denial of His signs, which are set up for reflection and sent down from Him, since the wording of the verse encompasses that.

The Quranic commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on surah 41, verses 16–18:

God the Exalted said:

﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind during days of ill omen, that We might make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world. But the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing, and they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them for what they had earned.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to be mindful of God.﴾

It has been related in a ḥadīth: "God the Exalted commanded the keepers of the wind, and they opened upon ʿĀd from it an amount equal to the ring of a seal. Had they opened an amount equal to the nostril of a bull, the world would have been destroyed." And it has been related that "the wind would lift up the caravan with its loads, and send it flying, until it cast it into the sea." Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh and al-Taymī said: "Rain was withheld from them for three years. When God wills evil for a people, He withholds rain from them and sends the wind upon them."

People differed concerning ṣarṣar (furious). Qatādah, al-Suddī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is derived from ṣirr, which is cold, and the meaning is: a cold wind that has a sound. Mujāhid said: ṣarṣar means intensely hot, scorching winds upon them. al-Ṭabarī and a group of exegetes said: it is from ṣarṣara, when it makes a sound resembling the sounds of ṣād and rāʾ, and in this way the sound of the wind often comes, according to what it encounters.

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, al-Aʿraj, al-Nakhaʿī and ʿĪsā read "naḥsāt" (ill-omened) with a sukūn on the ḥāʾ. It is the plural of naḥs, as one says yawm naḥs (an ill-omened day) and qawm naḥs (an ill-omened people). It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) which is sometimes used as an attribute and sometimes is idafa'd to "al-yawm." Here it was pluralized as an attribute. Abū ʿAmr argued for this reading with God's words: ﴿on a day of continuous ill omen﴾ (al-Qamar 19). Al-Nakhaʿī said: "naḥasāt, and not naḥisāt with a kasra on the ḥāʾ." The rest of the readers, along with Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, Abū Rajāʾ, Qatādah, al-Jaḥdarī and al-Aʿmash, read "naḥisāt" with a kasra on the ḥāʾ. It is the plural of naḥis, on the pattern of ḥadhir, and it is an attribute of the day, derived from al-naḥs (ill omen). al-Ṭabarī said: naḥis and naḥs are two dialects.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

That is not so. Rather, one language encompasses both: one of them is a maṣdar and the other is from the patterns of the active participle (ism al-fāʿil). al-Farrāʾ recited:

*Inform Judhām and Lakhm that their brothers,*
*Ṭayy and Bahrāʾ, are a people whose helper is an ill-omened one.*

(p-472) A group said: "naḥsāt" with the sukūn is a lightened form of "naḥisāt" with the kasra, and the meaning of this word is: ill-omened (mashāʾim), from the well-known naḥs. This was said by Mujāhid, Qatādah and al-Suddī. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: its meaning is: severe, that is, severe in cold, to the point that the cold was a punishment for them. Abū ʿAlī said: al-Aṣmaʿī recited, using naḥs in the sense of cold:

*As if a pure wine had been displayed to a naḥs (cold),*
*whose clarity makes the clear water appear [like it].*

Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: "naḥisāt" means successive, and it was from the last Wednesday of Shawwāl to the following Wednesday.

"The punishment of disgrace in the life of this world" is destruction because of disbelief and opposition to God's command, and there is no greater disgrace than this, except what is in the Hereafter of eternal abiding in the Fire.

The majority of people read ﴿"wa-amma Thamūd"﴾ without tanwīn, and this is taken as referring to the tribe. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, al-Aʿmash and Bakr ibn Ḥabīb read "wa-amma Thamūdun" with tanwīn and with inflection, and this is taken as referring to the living group. Al-Aʿmash and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb used to read with the diacritics throughout the Qurʾan, except in God's words ﴿And We gave Thamūd the she-camel﴾ (al-Isrāʾ 59), because it is written in the muṣḥaf without an alif. Ibn Abī Isḥāq, al-Aʿraj (in one of two narrations), al-Aʿmash and ʿĀṣim read "Thamūda" in the accusative, and this is taken as the verb being implied by God's words ﴿so We guided them﴾ (fa-hadaynāhum). Its estimate according to Sībawayh is: "Whatever there may be, We guided Thamūd, [so] We guided them." The nominative, according to him, has several aspects. It was related from Ibn Abī Isḥāq and al-Aʿmash: "Thamūdan," with tanwīn and in the accusative. Al-Faḍl related from ʿĀṣim both readings.

God's words ﴿fa-hadaynāhum﴾ mean: We made clear to them. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Guidance here does not mean direction (irshād). It is like the way the Islamic law is now explained to the Jews and Christians who are mixed in with us, but they turn away and busy themselves with the opposite. That is "preferring blindness over guidance." God's words ﴿so they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ are an expression of their earning (taksub) in blindness; otherwise, it is by origination (ikhtirāʿ) from God the Exalted. What indicates that it refers to their earning is God's words ﴿for what they had been earning﴾. God's words ﴿the humiliating punishment﴾ are a description by the verbal noun (waṣf bi-l-maṣdar), and the meaning is: the punishment with which there is humiliation and abasement. Then God the Exalted joined with their mention the mention of those who believed, were mindful and were saved by it, in order to make the distinction clear.

God the Exalted said:

﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind during days of ill omen, that We might make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world. But the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing, and they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them for what they had earned.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to be mindful of God.﴾

It has been related in a ḥadīth: "God the Exalted commanded the keepers of the wind, and they opened upon ʿĀd from it an amount equal to the ring of a seal. Had they opened an amount equal to the nostril of a bull, the world would have been destroyed." And it has been related that "the wind would lift up the caravan with its loads, and send it flying, until it cast it into the sea." Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh and al-Taymī said: "Rain was withheld from them for three years. When God wills evil for a people, He withholds rain from them and sends the wind upon them."

People differed concerning ṣarṣar (furious). Qatādah, al-Suddī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is derived from ṣirr, which is cold, and the meaning is: a cold wind that has a sound. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verse 19–22:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿On the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, they will be marshalled in ranks.﴾ ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why do you testify against us?" They will say, "Allah has made us speak, who makes everything speak, and He created you the first time, and to Him you will be returned."﴾ ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins should testify against you, but you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do.﴾

[Wa-yawma] is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is: "Remember the day when..." Nafi' alone, al-A'raj, and the people of Madina read "nahshuru" with the nun, [a'da'a] in the accusative, except that al-A'raj vowelled the shin with a kasra. The rest read "yuhsharu" with a raised ya', "a'da'u" in the nominative, and this is the reading of al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far, Qatada, 'Isa, Talha, and Nafi' according to what has been related from him. Its proof is [yuza'una]. "A'da'u Allah" are the disbelievers who oppose His command. [Yuza'una], Qatada and the lexicographers said: their first is held back so that the last of them is restrained (yukaffu awwaluhum habsan 'ala akhirihim). In the hadith of Abu Quhafa on the day of the conquest: "That is the restrainer (al-wazi')." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: a judge must have guards (wazaha). Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (p-474) may Allah be pleased with him said: "I will not exact retribution from the guards of Allah, the Exalted."

[Hatta] is the limit of this gathering mentioned, and this describes one of their states at some times of the Resurrection, namely when they reach Jahannam. Allah, the Exalted, will then cause them to acknowledge against themselves, and they will be asked a question of rebuke about their disbelief; they will deny it and suppose that there is no witness, and they will take the question to be one of inquiry and seeking information. So Allah, the Exalted, will make their limbs speak in testimony against them. It has been related from the Prophet ﷺ: "The first part of a person to speak is his left thigh, then the limbs speak, and the disbeliever will say: 'Woe to you, O limbs! It was on your behalf that I was defending myself.'" In another hadith: "They will come on the Day of Resurrection with their mouths sealed, and the thigh and the palm will speak."

Then Allah, the Exalted, mentioned their dialogue with their skins in their saying: ﴿Why do you testify against us?﴾, meaning: "And our punishment is a punishment for you." People differed about what is meant by the skins. The majority of people said: they are the well-known skins. 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far said: by "skins" He meant the private parts, and it is these that were intended. Allah, the Exalted, informed that the skins will answer their reply that Allah, the Exalted, the Creator, the Originator, the Restorer, is He who made them speak. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿who made everything speak﴾ means: every thing that speaks, whether that is by ordinary custom or by a breach of custom.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves﴾ may be from the speech of the skins and their dialogue, and it may be from the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to them, or from the speech of an angel commanded by Him. As for the meaning, it allows two aspects. One of them is that it means: "And you were not guarding yourselves and restraining your souls from sins and disbelief for fear that you would be witnessed against, or for the sake of not being witnessed against, but you thought that Allah, glorified is He, does not know, so you plunged in and openly defied." This is the view of Mujahid, and the word "al-sitr" (concealment) may be used in this meaning and similar, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Concealment is what stands between one and the immoral acts, and what meets you, short of good, is not a concealment."

The second meaning is that it means: "And you were not able to refrain, and it was not possible for you, nor did you have the capacity, to hide from your limbs and conceal yourselves from them by your disbelief and your sins, and you did not think that they would reach this extent." This is the view of al-Suddi, as if the meaning is: "And you did not ward off by hiding and concealment that they would witness, because the limbs are bound to you." In obliging them to the assumption that Allah, the Exalted, does not know, there is an obligation of disbelief and ignorance of Allah, the Exalted, and this belief leads its holder to denying the commands of the messengers and belittling the power of Allah, the Exalted, there is no lord but Him. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: [But you supposed that Allah]. Al-Tabari related from Qatada that he expressed "tastatirun" as "tazunnun" (you suppose), and that is an explanation in which the wording was not considered and there is no connection with it. Al-Tabari and others mentioned a hadith: "From 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I was hidden behind the curtains of the Ka'ba when three men entered, two Qurashis and a Thaqafi, or two Thaqafis and a Qurashi, little understanding in their hearts, much fat in their bellies. They talked about something, and one of them said: 'Do you think Allah hears what we say?' Another said: 'He hears if we raise our voices, and does not hear if we lower them.' Another said: 'If He hears any of it, He hears all of it.' So I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him of that, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves﴾ up to where He recited ﴿And if they ask to be shown favour, they will not be among those shown favour﴾ [Fussilat: 24]." Al-Tha'labi mentioned that the Thaqafi was 'Abd Yalil, and the two Qurashis were his brothers-in-law: Rabi'a and Safwan, the two sons of Umayya ibn Khalaf.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems that this was after the conquest of Makka, and the verse is Madani. It seems that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited the verse as an illustration when 'Abd Allah informed him, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verse 19–22:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿On the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, they will be marshalled in ranks.﴾ ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why do you testify against us?" They will say, "Allah has made us speak, who makes everything speak, and He created you the first time, and to Him you will be returned."﴾ ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins should testify against you, but you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do.﴾

[Wa-yawma] is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is: "Remember the day when..." Nafi' alone, al-A'raj, and the people of Madina read "nahshuru" with the nun, [a'da'a] in the accusative, except that al-A'raj vowelled the shin with a kasra. The rest read "yuhsharu" with a raised ya', "a'da'u" in the nominative, and this is the reading of al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far, Qatada, 'Isa, Talha, and Nafi' according to what has been related from him. Its proof is [yuza'una]. "A'da'u Allah" are the disbelievers who oppose His command. [Yuza'una], Qatada and the lexicographers said: their first is held back so that the last of them is restrained (yukaffu awwaluhum habsan 'ala akhirihim). In the hadith of Abu Quhafa on the day of the conquest: "That is the restrainer (al-wazi')." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: a judge must have guards (wazaha). Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (p-474) may Allah be pleased with him said: "I will not exact retribution from the guards of Allah, the Exalted."

[Hatta] is the limit of this gathering mentioned, and this describes one of their states at some times of the Resurrection, namely when they reach Jahannam. Allah, the Exalted, will then cause them to acknowledge against themselves, and they will be asked a question of rebuke about their disbelief; they will deny it and suppose that there is no witness, and they will take the question to be one of inquiry and seeking information. So Allah, the Exalted, will make their limbs speak in testimony against them. It has been related from the Prophet ﷺ: "The first part of a person to speak is his left thigh, then the limbs speak, and the disbeliever will say: 'Woe to you, O limbs! It was on your behalf that I was defending myself.'" In another hadith: "They will come on the Day of Resurrection with their mouths sealed, and the thigh and the palm will speak."

Then Allah, the Exalted, mentioned their dialogue with their skins in their saying: ﴿Why do you testify against us?﴾, meaning: "And our punishment is a punishment for you." People differed about what is meant by the skins. The majority of people said: they are the well-known skins. 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far said: by "skins" He meant the private parts, and it is these that were intended. Allah, the Exalted, informed that the skins will answer their reply that Allah, the Exalted, the Creator, the Originator, the Restorer, is He who made them speak. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿who made everything speak﴾ means: every thing that speaks, whether that is by ordinary custom or by a breach of custom.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves﴾ may be from the speech of the skins and their dialogue, and it may be from the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to them, or from the speech of an angel commanded by Him. As for the meaning, it allows two aspects. One of them is that it means: "And you were not guarding yourselves and restraining your souls from sins and disbelief for fear that you would be witnessed against, or for the sake of not being witnessed against, but you thought that Allah, glorified is He, does not know, so you plunged in and openly defied." This is the view of Mujahid, and the word "al-sitr" (concealment) may be used in this meaning and similar, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Concealment is what stands between one and the immoral acts, and what meets you, short of good, is not a concealment."

The second meaning is that it means: "And you were not able to refrain, and it was not possible for you, nor did you have the capacity, to hide from your limbs and conceal yourselves from them by your disbelief and your sins, and you did not think that they would reach this extent." This is the view of al-Suddi, as if the meaning is: "And you did not ward off by hiding and concealment that they would witness, because the limbs are bound to you." In obliging them to the assumption that Allah, the Exalted, does not know, there is an obligation of disbelief and ignorance of Allah, the Exalted, and this belief leads its holder to denying the commands of the messengers and belittling the power of Allah, the Exalted, there is no lord but Him. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: [But you supposed that Allah]. Al-Tabari related from Qatada that he expressed "tastatirun" as "tazunnun" (you suppose), and that is an explanation in which the wording was not considered and there is no connection with it. Al-Tabari and others mentioned a hadith: "From 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I was hidden behind the curtains of the Ka'ba when three men entered, two Qurashis and a Thaqafi, or two Thaqafis and a Qurashi, little understanding in their hearts, much fat in their bellies. They talked about something, and one of them said: 'Do you think Allah hears what we say?' Another said: 'He hears if we raise our voices, and does not hear if we lower them.' Another said: 'If He hears any of it, He hears all of it.' So I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him of that, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves﴾ up to where He recited ﴿And if they ask to be shown favour, they will not be among those shown favour﴾ [Fussilat: 24]." Al-Tha'labi mentioned that the Thaqafi was 'Abd Yalil, and the two Qurashis were his brothers-in-law: Rabi'a and Safwan, the two sons of Umayya ibn Khalaf.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems that this was after the conquest of Makka, and the verse is Madani. It seems that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited the verse as an illustration when 'Abd Allah informed him, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verses 23–26:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿And that is your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has destroyed you, and you have become among the losers.﴾ ﴿So if they endure, the Fire is their abode; and if they ask to be restored to favour, they will not be among those granted it.﴾ ﴿And We appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them, and the word became due against them, among nations that had passed away before them of jinn and mankind. Indeed, they were losers.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it that you may overcome."﴾

[Dhalikum] is in the nominative as the subject of inception (mubtada'), and the reference of "that" is to His saying, "But you assumed that Allah does not know" [Fussilat: 22]. Qatadah said: "Assumption is of two kinds: an assumption that saves and an assumption that destroys."

[p. 477] The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The one that saves is that the monotheist who knows his Lord assumes that Allah the Exalted will have mercy on him. The one that destroys is the assumptions of the disbelievers, who are ignorant, in all their varieties. On this meaning, Yahya ibn Aktham has a fine and comforting dream.

[Zannukum] is the predicate of the inceptive subject (khabar mubtada').

His saying, ﴿[aradakum]﴾, may be a predicate following another predicate. The Kufans permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), but the Basrans do not permit the past tense to occur as a circumstantial accusative when it is preceded by qad. You say: "I saw Zayd, having (qad) stood." It is permissible, in their view, that it be taken as having qad implied even if it is not expressed. The meaning of ﴿[aradakum]﴾ is "destroyed you," and al-radaa (the ruin) is destruction.

His saying, ﴿So if they endure﴾, is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the meaning is: whether they endure or do not endure. He limited the statement to what is apparent in order to indicate what was omitted. "Al-mathwa" is the place of residence.

Most of the reciters read ﴿"wa-in yasta'tibu"﴾ with a fatha on the yaa and a kasra on the final taa, attributing the verb to them, and ﴿"fa-ma hum mina al-mu'tabina"﴾ with a fatha on the taa, meaning: even if they seek al-'utba, which is contentment, they are not among those who are given it and deserve it. Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Musa al-Aswari read ﴿"yusta'tabu"﴾ with a damma on the yaa and a fatha on the second taa, and ﴿"fa-ma hum mina al-mu'tibina"﴾ with a kasra on the taa, meaning: even if good or reform is requested of them, they are not among those in whom it is found, because they have departed the world, the abode of works. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "There is no seeking of restoration after death." It is possible that this reading means: even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden.

Then the Exalted described their state in the world and what befell them when they turned away, so He decreed the judgment against them.

[Qayyadna] means: We facilitated for them evil companions from the devils and the misguided among mankind. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and they made attractive to them what was before them﴾ means: they taught them and established in their souls evil beliefs concerning matters that preceded them, such as the affair of the Messengers, peace be upon them, prophethood, praising the worship of idols, following the practice of their fathers, and other things of which it is said, "it is before them." This is everything that preceded them in time and whose effect or report reached them. Likewise, they gave them evil beliefs about what is behind them, which is everything that will come after them, such as the Resurrection, the raising, and similar things of which it is said, "it is behind man." So they made attractive to them, in these two matters, everything that would ruin them and lead them to the punishment of Hell.

His saying, ﴿and the word became due against them﴾, means: the preceding of the decisive decree and the command of Allah to punish them, among a group of nations who were punished, disbelievers, from the jinn and mankind. A group has said: [fi] here has the meaning of [ma'a] ("with").

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is fulfilled with the two particles, and we do not need to make one particle carry the meaning of another, since the leading Basran grammarians have rejected that.

His saying, ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Do not listen to this Qur'an"﴾, is a report of what some of the Quraysh did, such as Abu Jahl and others. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite the Qur'an in the Sacred Mosque, and people, both believers and disbelievers, would listen to him. The disbelievers feared that the hearts would be drawn to it, so they said: "Whenever Muhammad recites, let us drown him out with whistling, clapping and shouting, and reciting poetry and rajaz, until his voice is concealed and he cannot be heard." This act of theirs is the "laghw" (idle noise). Abu al-'Aliyah said: they meant: "Find fault with it and disparage it." "Al-laghw" in the language is the useless speech that has no meaning, and it comes from frivolity and prolixity about a matter that has no meaning.

Most of the reciters read ﴿[wa-lghaw]﴾ with a fatha on the ghayn and a jazm on the waw. Bakr ibn Habib al-Sahmi read "wa-lghu" with a damma on the ghayn and a sukun on the waw, and it is reported from 'Isa and Ibn Abi Ishaq (with a difference of transmission from them), and both are dialectal forms. It is said: lagha yalghu, and it is also said: laghiya yalgha, and also: lagha yalgha. The original form is yaf'ilu (with a kasra on the ayn), but the throat letter brought it back to the fatha. So the first reading is from yalgha, and the second reading is from yalghu, as stated by al-Akhfash.

His saying, ﴿so that you may overcome﴾, means: that you may obliterate the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ), cause his remembrance to die out, and divert hearts away from him. This is the aim they hoped for.

His saying, ﴿and the word became due against them﴾, means: the preceding of the decisive decree and the command of Allah to punish them, among a group of nations who were punished, disbelievers, from the jinn and mankind. A group has said: [fi] here has the meaning of [ma'a] ("with").

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is fulfilled with the two particles, and we do not need to make one particle carry the meaning of another, since the leading Basran grammarians have rejected that.

His saying, ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Do not listen to this Qur'an"﴾, is a report of what some of the Quraysh did, such as Abu Jahl and others. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite the Qur'an in the Sacred Mosque, and people, both believers and disbelievers, would listen to him. The disbelievers feared that the hearts would be drawn to it, so they said: "Whenever Muhammad recites, let us drown him out with whistling, clapping and shouting, and reciting poetry and rajaz, until his voice is concealed and he cannot be heard." This act of theirs is the "laghw" (idle noise). Abu al-'Aliyah said: they meant: "Find fault with it and disparage it." "Al-laghw" in the language is the useless speech that has no meaning, and it comes from frivolity and prolixity about a matter that has no meaning.

Most of the reciters read ﴿[wa-lghaw]﴾ with a fatha on the ghayn and a jazm on the waw. Bakr ibn Habib al-Sahmi read "wa-lghu" with a damma on the ghayn and a sukun on the waw, and it is reported from 'Isa and Ibn Abi Ishaq (with a difference of transmission from them), and both are dialectal forms. It is said: lagha yalghu, and it is also said: laghiya yalgha, and also: lagha yalgha. The original form is yaf'ilu (with a kasra on the ayn), but the throat letter brought it back to the fatha. So the first reading is from yalgha, and the second reading is from yalghu, as stated by al-Akhfash.

His saying, ﴿so that you may overcome﴾, means: that you may obliterate the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ), cause his remembrance to die out, and divert hearts away from him. This is the aim they hoped for.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verse 27–30:

(p-479) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire; for them therein is the abode of eternity; a recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieved will say: "Our Lord, show us those who misled us of the jinn and mankind, that we may place them under our feet so they will be among the lowest."﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remained steadfast – the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, and receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised."﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste﴾ The fa' (فَ) is attached to the lam of oath (لامِ القَسَمِ), and it is a verse of threat to Quraysh. The "severe punishment" is the punishment of this world, at Badr and other than it, and "the recompense with the worst of their deeds" is the punishment of the Hereafter.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"That" [dhālika]﴾ is a reference to the previously mentioned recompense, and "recompense" (jazā') is the predicate of the subject, and "the Fire" (al-nār) is an apposition (badal) to His saying "recompense." It is permissible that "that" (dhālika) be the predicate of an inchoative subject, its estimate being: "the matter is that," and His saying "recompense" is then an inchoative subject and "the Fire" is its predicate. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿for them therein is the abode of eternity⦆ meaning: a place of remaining and a dwelling of everlasting punishment. The adverbial sense (ẓarfiyya) in it is established according to this interpretation. It is also possible that the meaning is: "it is for them the abode of eternity," so in His saying "therein" (fīhā) there is the sense of specification (taḥdīd), as the poet said:

؎ And in God, if they do not act justly, there is a just judge

(p-480) In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd: [That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire, the abode of eternity], and "for them therein" is omitted. Their denial of the signs of Allah is constant, in His markers set up for His creation and in the signs of His Book revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ).

Then the Mighty and Majestic mentioned the statement of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when they enter the Fire; they see the magnitude of what has befallen them and the evil of their final place of return. Their thoughts roam over those who were the cause of their misguidance and the origin of their error, so their anger and rage against him greatly intensify, and they wish that he would receive the most severe punishment. Then they say: ﴿Our Lord, show us those who misled us﴾. The apparent wording requires that "the one" (alladhī) in their saying [alladhīna] is for the category, meaning: show us every misguider and misleader among the jinn and mankind. This is the view of a group of exegetes. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Qatāda said: they sought the son of Ādam who established killing and disobedience among humans, and Iblīs, the father of devils, among the jinn.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Consider this: is this authentically reported from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him? For the son of Ādam is a believing sinner, whereas these only sought those who misled them into disbelief which leads to eternity. The stronger view is that they sought both types. Some have refined this view by saying: every sinner among the people of major sins who enters the Fire seeks the son of Ādam, and every disbeliever seeks Iblīs. But the wording of the verse contradicts this interpretation, since it requires that the disbelievers only sought the two who misled them.

Nāfiʿ, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read: ﴿Arinā﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ, and it is a sight of the eye (ruʾyat ʿayn), and for this reason it is a verb transitive to two objects. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim read: ﴿Arinā﴾ with a sukūn on the rāʾ. Hishām ibn ʿĀmir said: it is an error. Abū ʿAlī said: it is a lightened form of "Arinā," as they said "ḍaḥk" and "fakhdh" (lightened forms of ḍaḥik and fakhidh). Abū ʿAmr read with ishmām of the rāʾ toward kasra, and this was transmitted from the people of Makkah. Their saying: ﴿that we may place them under our feet﴾ means: at the lowest level of the Fire, which is more severe in punishment, and it is the abyss of the hypocrites.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remained steadfast﴾ is a verse. It is a verse of promise for the believers.

(p-481) Sufyān ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Thaqafī said: "I said to the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace: Inform me of a matter to which I may hold fast. He said: Say, 'My Lord is Allah,' then be steadfast. I said: What do you fear most for me? So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took hold of his own tongue and said: This."

People differed regarding the implication of His saying: ﴿then remained steadfast﴾. al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and a group held that its meaning is: they remained steadfast in acts of obedience and avoidance of sins. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, recited this verse on the pulpit and then said: "By Allah, they remained steadfast for Allah in His obedience, and they did not swerve like foxes."

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He, may Allah be pleased with him, sought to apply the statement to the most complete and most excellent sense; otherwise, according to this interpretation, it would follow from its implicit meaning that the angels do not descend at death upon someone who is not steadfast in obedience. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, and a group with him held that the meaning is: they remained steadfast upon their saying "Our Lord is Allah," so their monotheism did not waver and their faith was not disturbed. Anas ibn Mālik narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse and said: "People have said it, then most of them disbelieved; so whoever dies upon it, he is among those who were steadfast."

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning: he is at the first level of steadfastness, safe from eternal abode. This is like his saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "Whoever's last words are 'There is no god but Allah' enters Paradise." This is the belief, God willing, because the sinners of the Ummah of Muḥammad (ﷺ) and others are of two groups: as for the one for whom Allah has decreed forgiveness and the abandonment of his punishment, he is without doubt among those upon whom the angels descend with glad tidings, for he has remained steadfast only in his monotheism. As for the one for whom Allah has decreed punishment for a period, then his admission to Paradise, (p-482) he will without doubt encounter all of that at his death and know it. It is not valid that his state be like the state of the disbeliever who despairs of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted. Since this is so, he has received the glad tidings that he will not fear eternity nor grieve over it, and that he will ultimately arrive at eternity in Paradise. Are not the believing sinners only under the promise of Paradise? They are among those to whom it is said: ﴿And receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised.﴾ Notwithstanding all this, there is no disagreement that the monotheist who is steadfast in obedience is in a more complete state and has a more perfect glad tiding, and this is the aim of the Commander of the Faithful ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him. In a similar vein, Sufyān al-Thawrī said: "They remained steadfast" means: they acted in accordance with what they said. al-Rabīʿ said: they turned away from all besides Allah, the Exalted. al-Faḍl said: they renounced the transient and desired the lasting. In sum, the more a person is prepared, the swifter he is to attain the grace of Allah, the Exalted.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾ is a general assurance against every future worry and a complete consolation for everything lost in the past. Mujāhid said: the meaning is: do not fear what you are about to face, and do not grieve over what you left behind of your worldly life. In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him: [the angels descend upon them, "Do not fear"], with the alif dropped, meaning: they say, "Do not fear."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verse 27–30:

(p-479) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire; for them therein is the abode of eternity; a recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieved will say: "Our Lord, show us those who misled us of the jinn and mankind, that we may place them under our feet so they will be among the lowest."﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remained steadfast – the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, and receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised."﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste﴾ The fa' (فَ) is attached to the lam of oath (لامِ القَسَمِ), and it is a verse of threat to Quraysh. The "severe punishment" is the punishment of this world, at Badr and other than it, and "the recompense with the worst of their deeds" is the punishment of the Hereafter.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"That" [dhālika]﴾ is a reference to the previously mentioned recompense, and "recompense" (jazā') is the predicate of the subject, and "the Fire" (al-nār) is an apposition (badal) to His saying "recompense." It is permissible that "that" (dhālika) be the predicate of an inchoative subject, its estimate being: "the matter is that," and His saying "recompense" is then an inchoative subject and "the Fire" is its predicate. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿for them therein is the abode of eternity⦆ meaning: a place of remaining and a dwelling of everlasting punishment. The adverbial sense (ẓarfiyya) in it is established according to this interpretation. It is also possible that the meaning is: "it is for them the abode of eternity," so in His saying "therein" (fīhā) there is the sense of specification (taḥdīd), as the poet said:

؎ And in God, if they do not act justly, there is a just judge

(p-480) In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd: [That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire, the abode of eternity], and "for them therein" is omitted. Their denial of the signs of Allah is constant, in His markers set up for His creation and in the signs of His Book revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ).

Then the Mighty and Majestic mentioned the statement of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when they enter the Fire; they see the magnitude of what has befallen them and the evil of their final place of return. Their thoughts roam over those who were the cause of their misguidance and the origin of their error, so their anger and rage against him greatly intensify, and they wish that he would receive the most severe punishment. Then they say: ﴿Our Lord, show us those who misled us﴾. The apparent wording requires that "the one" (alladhī) in their saying [alladhīna] is for the category, meaning: show us every misguider and misleader among the jinn and mankind. This is the view of a group of exegetes. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Qatāda said: they sought the son of Ādam who established killing and disobedience among humans, and Iblīs, the father of devils, among the jinn.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Consider this: is this authentically reported from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him? For the son of Ādam is a believing sinner, whereas these only sought those who misled them into disbelief which leads to eternity. The stronger view is that they sought both types. Some have refined this view by saying: every sinner among the people of major sins who enters the Fire seeks the son of Ādam, and every disbeliever seeks Iblīs. But the wording of the verse contradicts this interpretation, since it requires that the disbelievers only sought the two who misled them.

Nāfiʿ, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read: ﴿Arinā﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ, and it is a sight of the eye (ruʾyat ʿayn), and for this reason it is a verb transitive to two objects. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim read: ﴿Arinā﴾ with a sukūn on the rāʾ. Hishām ibn ʿĀmir said: it is an error. Abū ʿAlī said: it is a lightened form of "Arinā," as they said "ḍaḥk" and "fakhdh" (lightened forms of ḍaḥik and fakhidh). Abū ʿAmr read with ishmām of the rāʾ toward kasra, and this was transmitted from the people of Makkah. Their saying: ﴿that we may place them under our feet﴾ means: at the lowest level of the Fire, which is more severe in punishment, and it is the abyss of the hypocrites.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remained steadfast﴾ is a verse. It is a verse of promise for the believers.

(p-481) Sufyān ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Thaqafī said: "I said to the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace: Inform me of a matter to which I may hold fast. He said: Say, 'My Lord is Allah,' then be steadfast. I said: What do you fear most for me? So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took hold of his own tongue and said: This."

People differed regarding the implication of His saying: ﴿then remained steadfast﴾. al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and a group held that its meaning is: they remained steadfast in acts of obedience and avoidance of sins. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, recited this verse on the pulpit and then said: "By Allah, they remained steadfast for Allah in His obedience, and they did not swerve like foxes."

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He, may Allah be pleased with him, sought to apply the statement to the most complete and most excellent sense; otherwise, according to this interpretation, it would follow from its implicit meaning that the angels do not descend at death upon someone who is not steadfast in obedience. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, and a group with him held that the meaning is: they remained steadfast upon their saying "Our Lord is Allah," so their monotheism did not waver and their faith was not disturbed. Anas ibn Mālik narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse and said: "People have said it, then most of them disbelieved; so whoever dies upon it, he is among those who were steadfast."

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning: he is at the first level of steadfastness, safe from eternal abode. This is like his saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "Whoever's last words are 'There is no god but Allah' enters Paradise." This is the belief, God willing, because the sinners of the Ummah of Muḥammad (ﷺ) and others are of two groups: as for the one for whom Allah has decreed forgiveness and the abandonment of his punishment, he is without doubt among those upon whom the angels descend with glad tidings, for he has remained steadfast only in his monotheism. As for the one for whom Allah has decreed punishment for a period, then his admission to Paradise, (p-482) he will without doubt encounter all of that at his death and know it. It is not valid that his state be like the state of the disbeliever who despairs of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted. Since this is so, he has received the glad tidings that he will not fear eternity nor grieve over it, and that he will ultimately arrive at eternity in Paradise. Are not the believing sinners only under the promise of Paradise? They are among those to whom it is said: ﴿And receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised.﴾ Notwithstanding all this, there is no disagreement that the monotheist who is steadfast in obedience is in a more complete state and has a more perfect glad tiding, and this is the aim of the Commander of the Faithful ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him. The Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 41, verses 31–35:

The Almighty's saying:

﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. Therein you will have whatever your souls desire, and therein you will have whatever you ask for.﴾ ﴿An accommodation from the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"?﴾ ﴿Good and evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with what is better, and thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend.﴾ ﴿But none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune.﴾

The speaker of "We are your allies" are the angels, who say, "Do not fear and do not grieve." That is, they say to the believers at death and at the moment of witnessing the Truth: "We were your allies in the world, and we are your allies in the Hereafter." Al-Suddi said: the meaning is, "We are your guardians in the world and your allies in the Hereafter." The pronoun in their saying ﴿"therein"﴾ refers to the Hereafter. "Tadda'un" means "you ask for" (taṭlubūn). "Nuzulan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). The recitation of the majority (qira'at al-Jumhur) is with a ḍamma on the zay, while Abu Haywa read it with sukoon.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And who is better in speech...﴾ — the verse is an opening exhortation addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ). Its wording is general, encompassing everyone who has called to Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and to obedience to Him, both in the past and in the present, from among the prophets (peace be upon them) and the believers. The meaning is: no one is better in speech than one whose condition is this. The scholars who held the verse to be general include al-Hasan (al-Basri), Muqatil, and a group. Others explained that the condition of Muhammad (ﷺ) was clearly of this kind, and that the verse was specifically about him; this was the view of al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Sirin. Qays ibn Abi Hazim, 'A'isha, Mother of the Believers (may Allah be pleased with her), and 'Ikrima said: this verse was revealed about the muadhdhins (those who call the adhan). Qays said: "and does righteous deeds" refers to the prayer between the adhan and the iqama. Al-Naqqash reported this from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The meaning of the view that it concerns the muadhdhins is that they are included in it. As for its revelation, it was in Makkah without any disagreement, and there was no adhan in Makkah; it was only instituted in Madinah. Although the adhan is indeed a form of calling to Allah, it is only a part of it. Calling to Allah with strength, such as fighting the disbelievers, repelling tyrants, and restraining oppressors, and other such things, is of far greater value than undertaking the adhan, since it involves no hardship. The most correct view is that the verse was revealed in general terms. Zayd ibn 'Ali said: the meaning is "of those who called to Allah, the Exalted, with the sword."

The majority read ﴿"Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ with two nuns, while Ibn Abi 'Abla read [Inni min al-Muslimin] with one nun. Al-Fudayl ibn Rufayda said: "I was a muadhdhin among the companions of Ibn Mas'ud. 'Asim ibn Hubayra said to me: When you have completed the adhan, say, 'Indeed, I am of the Muslims,' and then he recited this verse."

Then the Exalted admonished His Prophet (peace be upon him), and directed him to the best form of address. He affirmed that good and evil are not equal, that is, the good is more excellent. He repeated "lā" in His saying ﴿and not evil﴾ for emphasis, to indicate that the intended meaning is: "good and evil are not equal, nor are evil and good." So the second term was omitted for brevity, and the [repeated] lā indicated this omission. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Repel [evil] with what is better﴾ is a verse that combines noble character and all kinds of forbearance. The meaning is: repel your affairs, and whatever confronts you with people and your dealings with them, with the conduct or manner that is the best of actions and dispositions. Among this is extending greetings of peace, good manners, restraining anger, generosity in repaying and in demanding repayment, and other things. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: when the believer practises these virtues, Allah protects him from Satan, and his enemy becomes submissive to him. Mujahid and 'Ata' interpreted this verse as referring to giving greetings of peace upon meeting.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

There is no doubt that greeting with peace is the starting point of repelling with what is better, and is a part of it.

Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿as though he were a devoted friend﴾. He introduced the particle of comparison (ka) because one who harbours enmity does not become a devoted friend; rather, his outward appearance is made to look good, and so he is compared to a devoted friend. The "ḥamīm" is the close relative who is dear to a person. The pronoun in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"it"﴾ refers to this disposition, which is implied by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Repel [evil] with what is better﴾. A group said: the meaning is "and it is not granted except to one who says there is no god but Allah." This is an interpretation that the wording does not require. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except those who are patient﴾ is an eloquent praise of patience, which is clear to the one who reflects, since patience in obedience and in restraint from desires encompasses all kinds of goodness. The phrase "a great portion" (ḥaẓẓ ʿaẓīm) may mean "of intellect and virtue," in which case the verse is praise. It has been reported that a man reviled Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Abu Bakr remained silent for a while; then anger surged in him, and he retaliated against the man. The Prophet (ﷺ) then stood up, and Abu Bakr followed him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, you stood up when I retaliated?" He said: "Indeed, an angel was repelling [the insults] from you, but when you began to retaliate, the angel departed and Satan came, and I would not sit with him." It may also mean "one of great fortune of Paradise and the reward of the Hereafter," in which case the verse is a promise. Qatada interpreted "ḥaẓẓ" here as Paradise.

The Almighty's saying:

Therein you will have whatever your souls desire, and therein you will have whatever you ask for.﴾ ﴿An accommodation from the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"?﴾ ﴿Good and evil are not equal. The speaker of "We are your allies" are the angels, who say, "Do not fear and do not grieve." That is, they say to the believers at death and at the moment of witnessing the Truth: "We were your allies in the world, and we are your allies in the Hereafter." "Tadda'un" means "you ask for" (taṭlubūn). "Nuzulan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). The recitation of the majority (qira'at al-Jumhur) is with a ḍamma on the zay, while Abu Haywa read it with sukoon.

Its wording is general, encompassing everyone who has called to Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and to obedience to Him, both in the past and in the present, from among the prophets (peace be upon them) and the believers. The meaning is: no one is better in speech than one whose condition is this. The scholars who held the verse to be general include al-Hasan (al-Basri), Muqatil, and a group. Others explained that the condition of Muhammad (ﷺ) was clearly of this kind, and that the verse was specifically about him; this was the view of al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Sirin. The majority read ﴿"Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ with two nuns, while Ibn Abi 'Abla read [Inni min al-Muslimin] with one nun. Al-Fudayl ibn Rufayda said: "I was a muadhdhin among the companions of Ibn Mas'ud. (p-485) The words of the Exalted:

﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should stir you, seek refuge in God; indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate yourselves to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate yourselves to God who created them, if it is Him that you worship.﴾ ﴿So if they are arrogant, those who are with your Lord glorify Him night and day, and they never tire.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed He who revives it is the reviver of the dead. Indeed He is over all things omnipotent.﴾

[Idha] is a conditional particle (shart), and the answer to the condition is the Exalted's words: ﴿[fa-ista'idh] (seek refuge)﴾. Al-nazgh (the prompting) is the act of Satan upon the heart or the hand, through the instilling of anger, rancour, or violence in the hand. From anger comes this verse; from rancour comes the Exalted's words: ﴿Satan incited discord between me and my brothers﴾ [Yusuf: 100]; and from violence comes the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let none of you point with a weapon at his brother, for Satan may stir in his hand, and he will fall into a pit of the pits of the Fire." In this preceding verse God urged towards noble character in repelling evil with what is better, then He praised those who attain it and promised them. He knew that human nature sometimes prevails and that people are stirred by the surge of anger and the prompting of Satan, so He guided them to the remedy for that, which is seeking refuge in Him, Mighty and Majestic.

Then He enumerated His signs so that whoever turns away from monotheism might take heed from them, by mentioning the night and the day. Mention of these two includes what is in them of shortening and lengthening, alternation and equality at times, and their other lessons. Likewise, the sun and the moon include their wonders, God's wisdom in them, and the benefit He gives His servants through them. Since it is said "shumus" (suns) and "aqmar" (moons) because they differ according to the days, it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the plural. The norm for the pronoun of non-rational beings is that when the number is less than ten, it comes in this form; when it exceeds ten, it is used in the feminine singular. So you say: "al-ajdhā' inkasarna" (the trunks broke, plural feminine) and "al-judhū' inkasarat" (the trunks broke, singular feminine). From this is the verse: ﴿Indeed the number of months﴾ [al-Tawba: 36], and from this is the verse of Hassan ibn Thabit:

*And our swords drip with blood from Najda.*

And al-Samaw'al said:

*There is no fault in us except that our swords,*
*with them are notches from the striking of the armoured warriors.*

(p-487) This is a common and well-known usage, though sometimes the matter is found overlapping, one part upon another.
