Then the Exalted mentioned a sign set up so that it might be taken as a lesson concerning the matter of resurrection from the graves, and so that what has been witnessed of this might be used as evidence for what has not yet been witnessed of that. The "humility (khushū') of the earth" is what appears upon it of abasement and dishevelment through barrenness and the scorching of hot winds; it is grim-faced, as the humble person is grim-faced, nearly weeping. "The water sent down" is rain. "The stirring (ihtizāz) of the earth" is the loosening of its parts by the water and its cracking for the plants. "Its swelling (rabwuhā)" is its inflation by the water and the rising of its surface by it. The majority (of reciters, al-jumhūr) read "wa-rabat" (and it swelled); Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "wa-raba'at" with a hamza after the alif, and it was transmitted by al-Rawasi from Abu 'Amr. (p-485) The words of the Exalted:

﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should stir you, seek refuge in God; indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate yourselves to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate yourselves to God who created them, if it is Him that you worship.﴾ ﴿So if they are arrogant, those who are with your Lord glorify Him night and day, and they never tire.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed He who revives it is the reviver of the dead. Indeed He is over all things omnipotent.﴾

[Idha] is a conditional particle (shart), and the answer to the condition is the Exalted's words: ﴿[fa-ista'idh] (seek refuge)﴾. Al-nazgh (the prompting) is the act of Satan upon the heart or the hand, through the instilling of anger, rancour, or violence in the hand. From anger comes this verse; from rancour comes the Exalted's words: ﴿Satan incited discord between me and my brothers﴾ [Yusuf: 100]; and from violence comes the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let none of you point with a weapon at his brother, for Satan may stir in his hand, and he will fall into a pit of the pits of the Fire." In this preceding verse God urged towards noble character in repelling evil with what is better, then He praised those who attain it and promised them. He knew that human nature sometimes prevails and that people are stirred by the surge of anger and the prompting of Satan, so He guided them to the remedy for that, which is seeking refuge in Him, Mighty and Majestic.

Then He enumerated His signs so that whoever turns away from monotheism might take heed from them, by mentioning the night and the day. Mention of these two includes what is in them of shortening and lengthening, alternation and equality at times, and their other lessons. Likewise, the sun and the moon include their wonders, God's wisdom in them, and the benefit He gives His servants through them. Then the Exalted said: Do not prostrate yourselves to these created things, even though they benefit you, because the benefit from them comes only through God's subjugation of them. It is He who should be prostrated to. As for the pronoun in ﴿"khalaqahunna" (He created them)﴾, one group said it refers to the days mentioned earlier; another group said it refers to the sun and the moon, and the two together are a plural, and the plural of non-rational beings takes the feminine, so He said "khalaqahunna."

(p-486) Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Since it is said "shumus" (suns) and "aqmar" (moons) because they differ according to the days, it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the plural. Another group said it refers to the four things mentioned. The norm for the pronoun of non-rational beings is that when the number is less than ten, it comes in this form; when it exceeds ten, it is used in the feminine singular. So you say: "al-ajdhā' inkasarna" (the trunks broke, plural feminine) and "al-judhū' inkasarat" (the trunks broke, singular feminine). From this is the verse: ﴿Indeed the number of months﴾ [al-Tawba: 36], and from this is the verse of Hassan ibn Thabit:

*And our swords drip with blood from Najda.*

And al-Samaw'al said:

*There is no fault in us except that our swords,*
*with them are notches from the striking of the armoured warriors.*

(p-487) This is a common and well-known usage, though sometimes the matter is found overlapping, one part upon another.

Then God addressed His Prophet (ﷺ) with words that include a warning to them and a belittling of their affair, and that God is not in need of their worship, by His words: ﴿So if they are arrogant﴾, the verse, and His words: ﴿Those who are with your Lord﴾, meaning by them the angels, who stand in rows and glorify. (p-489) Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Indeed, those who distort Our verses are not hidden from Us. So is one who is thrown into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection? Do what you will; indeed He is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them [will be punished]; and indeed it is a Mighty Book.﴾ ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it. It is a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you. Indeed your Lord is possessor of forgiveness and possessor of painful punishment.﴾

This is a verse of warning. "Al-ilhad" means inclining away, and here it means inclining away from the truth. From the same root comes "lahd" (the niche-grave dug in the side of a grave), because it lies on one side. It is said: "lahada al-rajul" and "alhada al-rajul" have the same meaning. The majority of reciters read ﴿"yulhidun"﴾ with a damma on the yā' (from alhada). Ibn Wthaab, Talhah, and al-A'mash read "yalhadun" with a fatha on the yā' and the ḥā' (from lahada).

The exegetes differed about what kind of ilhad is referred to. Qatadah and others said it is ilhad through denial. Mujahid and others said it is ilhad through whistling, clapping, and the idle talk they engaged in. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said their ilhad is placing speech in other than its proper place. The word ilhad covers all of this.

Allah's words ﴿they are not hidden from Us﴾ mean: We are watching them and We will punish them. Then Allah established, through these two categories, that they are [not equal]; and this establishing is what is meant here. That is, say to them, O Muhammad: [is one who ...]. Muqatil said this verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also said that it was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir (may Allah be pleased with him). The preference is stated here between being thrown into the Fire and being secure on the Day of Resurrection, even though the two do not share the quality of goodness. This is because the speech is an establishing and not merely a statement of fact, since the one who establishes a point may put his opponent to a choice between two options, one of which is clearly corrupt, so that he sees his answer. Perhaps he will fall into the corrupt meaning, and then his ignorance is made clear. The parallel of this verse and a full discussion of this meaning have already been mentioned. It is not appropriate here to say that He addressed them according to their belief, as that would be appropriate in His words ﴿better as a dwelling place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24]. So reflect on this. Allah's words ﴿Do what you will﴾ are a warning in the form of a command, by the consensus (ijma') of the scholars. The evidence for the warning and its clarification is His words ﴿indeed He is Seeing of what you do﴾.

(p-490) Then Allah said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them﴾, meaning the Quraysh. "Al-dhikr" is the Qur'an by consensus. People differed about where the predicate (khabar) of this statement is. One group said it is in His words ﴿They are called from a far place﴾ [Fussilat: 44]. al-Naqqash reported that Bilal ibn Abi Burdah asked about this in his assembly and said: "I have not found a way to make sense of it." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said to him: "It is indeed close to you: ﴿They are called﴾ [Fussilat: 44]."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This view is refuted by the great distance between the two parts, and because there are people who have responded well to this view by pointing to His words ﴿They are called﴾ [Fussilat: 44]. Another group said the predicate is implied, and its estimated form is: "Indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them perished or went astray." Some grammarians of Kufa said the response (jawab) is in His words ﴿and indeed it is a Mighty Book﴾. Al-Tabari reported this, and it is weak and not correct. 'Isa ibn 'Umar asked 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd about this, and 'Amr said: "Its meaning in tafsir is: Indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them, they disbelieved in it, and indeed it is a Mighty Book." 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: "You have done well, O Abu 'Uthman."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

What is best in this matter is that the predicate is implied, but at a place other than the one these scholars estimated. It is actually after ﴿All-Wise, Praiseworthy﴾, and this is more effective in showing the blame of the disbelievers for it. This is like saying: "Do you oppose Zayd, who is the knowing, the loving, the one whose matter and affair are such-and-such?" All of these are descriptions. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said its meaning is: honorable with Allah. Muqatil said: protected from Satan. al-Suddi said: uncreated.

Then Allah explained what was said to all of them, which is: ﴿Indeed your Lord is possessor of forgiveness﴾ for the obedient, ﴿and possessor of painful punishment﴾ for the disbelievers. In these words lies the totality of prohibition, reproof, and admonition, and to them every consideration returns.

From the same root comes "lahd" (the niche-grave dug in the side of a grave), because it lies on one side. It is said: "lahada al-rajul" and "alhada al-rajul" have the same meaning. The majority of reciters read ﴿"yulhidun"﴾ with a damma on the yā' (from alhada). Ibn Wthaab, Talhah, and al-A'mash read "yalhadun" with a fatha on the yā' and the ḥā' (from lahada).

The exegetes differed about what kind of ilhad is referred to. Qatadah and others said it is ilhad through denial. Mujahid and others said it is ilhad through whistling, clapping, and the idle talk they engaged in. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said their ilhad is placing speech in other than its proper place. The word ilhad covers all of this.

Allah's words ﴿they are not hidden from Us﴾ mean: We are watching them and We will punish them. Then Allah established, through these two categories, that they are [not equal]; and this establishing is what is meant here. That is, say to them, O Muhammad: [is one who ...]. Muqatil said this verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also said that it was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir (may Allah be pleased with him). The preference is stated here between being thrown into the Fire and being secure on the Day of Resurrection, even though the two do not share the quality of goodness. This is because the speech is an establishing and not merely a statement of fact, since the one who establishes a point may put his opponent to a choice between two options, one of which is clearly corrupt, so that he sees his answer. Perhaps he will fall into the corrupt meaning, and then his ignorance is made clear. The parallel of this verse and a full discussion of this meaning have already been mentioned. It is not appropriate here to say that He addressed them according to their belief, as that would be appropriate in His words ﴿better as a dwelling place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24]. So reflect on this. Allah's words ﴿Do what you will﴾ are a warning in the form of a command, by the consensus (ijma') of the scholars. The evidence for the warning and its clarification is His words ﴿indeed He is Seeing of what you do﴾.

(p-490) Then Allah said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them﴾, meaning the Quraysh. "Al-dhikr" is the Qur'an by consensus. People differed about where the predicate (khabar) of this statement is. One group said it is in His words ﴿They are called from a far place﴾ [Fussilat: 44]. al-Naqqash reported that Bilal ibn Abi Burdah asked about this in his assembly and said: "I have not found a way to make sense of it." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said to him: "It is indeed close to you: ﴿They are called﴾ [Fussilat: 44]."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This view is refuted by the great distance between the two parts, and because there are people who have responded well to this view by pointing to His words ﴿They are called﴾ [Fussilat: 44]. Another group said the predicate is implied, and its estimated form is: "Indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them perished or went astray." Some grammarians of Kufa said the response (jawab) is in His words ﴿and indeed it is a Mighty Book﴾. Al-Tabari reported this, and it is weak and not correct. 'Isa ibn 'Umar asked 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd about this, and 'Amr said: "Its meaning in tafsir is: Indeed those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them, they disbelieved in it, and indeed it is a Mighty Book." 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: "You have done well, O Abu 'Uthman."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

What is best in this matter is that the predicate is implied, but at a place other than the one these scholars estimated. It is actually after ﴿All-Wise, Praiseworthy﴾, and this is more effective in showing the blame of the disbelievers for it. This is because His words ﴿and indeed it is a Book﴾ belong to the description of the Reminder that they denied, so the mention of what is predicated is not complete until its description is completed. This is like saying: "Do you oppose Zayd, who is the knowing, the loving, the one whose matter and affair are such-and-such?" All of these are descriptions. Allah described the Book as Mighty because, through the soundness of its meanings, it is impervious to criticism and disparagement, and it is protected by Allah. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said its meaning is: honorable with Allah. Muqatil said: protected from Satan. al-Suddi said: uncreated.

(p-490) Allah's words ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it﴾: Qatadah and al-Suddi said it means Satan. The apparent wording is general, covering Satan and any matter that would invalidate any part of it. Allah's words ﴿from before it﴾ mean: there is nothing in the earlier books that invalidates any part of it. Allah's words ﴿or from behind it﴾ mean: no reflection of a reflective person and no thought of an intelligent person comes after it that would invalidate parts of it. The meaning of the wording as a whole is: falsehood cannot approach it from any direction. Allah's words ﴿"tanzil"﴾ are the predicate of an inchoative (mubtada') clause, meaning: it is a revelation.

Allah's words ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾ may have two meanings. The first is that it is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the speech of his people. That is: whatever harm you encounter from them, O Muhammad, and whatever painful words they say to you, they are only what was said and endured by the messengers before you. So take them as your example, persist in carrying out Allah's command, and do not be concerned by their affairs. The second meaning is that the verse is a clarification of the meanings of the Law (shar'): that is, what is said to you of revelation, through which you are addressed from Allah, is only what was said to the messengers before you. Then Allah explained what was said to all of them, which is: ﴿Indeed your Lord is possessor of forgiveness﴾ for the obedient, ﴿and possessor of painful punishment﴾ for the disbelievers. In these words lies the totality of prohibition, reproof, and admonition, and to them every consideration returns.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verses 44–46:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why are its verses not explained in detail? Is it non-Arabic and Arabic?" Say, "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. And as for those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them. Those are being called from a distant place."﴾ ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, but it was disputed over. And if not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them. And indeed they are, concerning it, in disquieting doubt.﴾ ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil, it is against it. And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾

Al-a'jami (the non-Arab, or that which is not clear in expression) is the one who does not speak clearly, whether Arab or non-Arab. Al-'ajami is one who is not of the Arabs, whether eloquent or not eloquent. This verse was revealed because of a confusion that came from Quraysh in their statements, concerning the letters that occurred in the Qur'an which had been Arabicized from the speech of non-Arabs, such as al-sijjin (سِجِّين) and al-istabraq (إسْتَبْرَق) and the like. So the Exalted and Majestic said: And if We had made this Qur'an non-Arabic, which does not clarify, they would have said and objected: "Why have You not made its verses clear?"

The readers differed concerning His saying: ﴿أأعْجَمِيٌّ وعَرَبِيٌّ﴾ (a'a'jamiyyun wa-'arabiyy). The reading of the majority is with the interrogative and a long hamza before the alif. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and al-A'mash read [أأعْجَمِيٌّ] with two hamzas. It seems they were rejecting this, saying: "Why was it not made clear? Is it non-Arabic and Arabic mixed? This is not fitting." Ibn Jubayr interpreted the meaning of their saying as: "Does non-Arabic foreignness come to us while we are Arabs? What have we to do with foreignness?" Al-Hasan al-Basri, Abu al-Aswad, al-Jahdari, Salam, al-Dahhak, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Amir, according to a variant from them, read [أعْجَمِيٌّ] without interrogation and with a sukun on the 'ayn, as though they said: "Foreignness and clarification?" This is indeed an anomalous reading. Or as though they said: "Why is it not distinguished into two parts, so that some of it is non-Arabic, understood by non-Arabs, and some of it is Arabic, understood by Arabs?" This is also an interpretation of Ibn Jubayr. 'Amr ibn Maymun read [أعَجَمِيٌّ] with a single hamza without a long vowel and with a fatha on the 'ayn. So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, informed about them that, had it been in any form imagined, they would have had a corrupt statement and objection. This is the purpose of the speech.

Allah, Exalted, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to say to them: Indeed, the Qur'an is guidance and healing for the believers who perceive the realities, and that it is, for those who do not believe and do not turn their sight and their senses toward created things, blindness; because in their ears is deafness, and upon their hearts are locks, and upon their eyes is a covering. People differed concerning His Exalted saying: ﴿وَهُوَ عَلَيْهِمْ عَمًى﴾ (and it is blindness for them). One group said: by "huwa" He means the Qur'an. Another group said: [wa-huwa] He means by it the deafness (al-waqr), and al-waqr is heaviness in the ear preventing hearing. All of these are metaphors; that is, when they did not understand and did not grasp, they were like the blind and the one with deafness. Ibn 'Abbas, Mu'awiya, and 'Amr ibn al-'As read [وَهُوَ عَلَيْهِمْ عَمٍ] with a kasra on the mim, nunated. Ya'qub said: "I do not know whether they nunated or made the ya' a fatha as a past verb." And without a ya', narrated by 'Amr ibn Dinar and Sulayman ibn Qatta from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. This reading also contains a metaphor. Likewise His Exalted saying: ﴿أُولَئِكَ يُنادَوْنَ﴾ (those are being called) admits two meanings, and both are stated by the exegetes. One is that it is a metaphor for the scarcity of their understanding: He likened them to a man who is called from a distance, hearing the voice from him but not understanding its details or its meanings. This is the interpretation of Mujahid. The other is that the speech is literal, and the meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection they will be called out with their disbelief and their evil deeds from a distance, so that the people of the gathering hear it, and their disgrace becomes great and their calamity descends. This is the interpretation of al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim.

Then the Exalted made the matter of Moses an example for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and for Quraysh; that is, the conduct of those (p-492) is like the conduct of these, when there came to them the like of what came to these. The "preceding word" is Allah the Exalted's decree to delay their punishment until the Day of Resurrection. The pronoun in His saying: ﴿لَفِي شَكٍّ مِنهُ﴾ (indeed, they are in doubt concerning it) may refer to Moses, peace be upon him, or to his Book.

As for His Exalted saying: ﴿مَن عَمِلَ صالِحًا فَلِنَفْسِهِ﴾ (whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul), the verse is a clear counsel to the worlds, a warning, a promise of hope, and a clear declaration that Allah, the Exalted, does not place any of the punishments of His servants other than in their proper place; rather He is the Just, the Bountiful, who recompenses every servant according to his earning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verses 47–50:

His, the Exalted's, saying:

﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour. No fruit emerges from its sheaths, no female conceives or gives birth, except with His knowledge. On the day He calls to them, "Where are My partners?" they will say, "We have declared to You that none of us bears witness."﴾ ﴿And what they used to invoke before has strayed from them, and they will realise that they have no place of escape.﴾ ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good, but if evil touches him, he is hopeless and despairing.﴾ ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, "This is mine, and I do not think the Hour will come. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him." But We will inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment.﴾

The meaning: the time of the knowledge of the Hour and its coming is referred by every believer who speaks about it to Allah, the Exalted and Majestic. He mentioned fruits and their emergence from their sheaths, and a female's bearing, as examples for all things, since everything hidden falls under the ruling of these two. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, al-Hasan, Talha and al-A'mash read "min thamarati" (from a fruit) in the singular, as a noun of genus. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "min thamarati" in the plural. The reading is disputed on the authority of 'Asim. It is also the reading of Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj and al-Hasan, with a variant. In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads "fi thamarah" (in a fruit). "Al-akmam" is the plural of "kumm" (sheath), which is the covering of the date-palm fruit before it appears.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And on the day He calls to them﴾ its implied meaning is: "and remember the day He calls to them." The pronoun in ﴿"calls to them"﴾ apparently and most naturally refers to the disbelievers who worship idols. It is possible that it refers to everyone who was worshipped besides Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, whether a human or other, but this is weak. As for the pronoun in His saying ﴿And what they used to invoke has strayed from them﴾, it can only refer to the disbelievers. As for ﴿"آذَنّاكَ"﴾ (we have declared to You), Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said its meaning is: "We have informed You that none of us witnesses, nor has anyone witnessed, that You have a partner." ﴿"And what has strayed from them"﴾ means they forgot what they used to say in the world and what they used to invoke of the deities and idols. It is possible that it means: the idols have gone astray from them, i.e., they have vanished from them, so they found no help from them, and their matter perished for them. His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿"And they realised"﴾ may be connected to what precedes it, with a pause upon it, and His, the Glorified's, saying ﴿"they have no place of escape"﴾ would be a resumption, denying that they have any refuge or place of evasion. You say "حاصَ الرَجُلُ" (the man evaded) when he turns aside seeking escape from something. From this is the hadith: "They fled in flight like wild donkeys toward the gates." On this interpretation, the verb "realised" (zanna) retains its original sense: they thought that this statement, "none of us bears witness," would be a means of escape for them, or a matter they used to disguise. It is also possible that the pause is at His saying ﴿"before"﴾, and ﴿"they realised"﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿"they have no place of escape"﴾, meaning: they realised that. On this interpretation, the verb "realised" carries the meaning of certainty, and al-Suddi interpreted it this way.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an expression that the people of the language use for "suspicion," but you will not find it used except for what is known with strong knowledge, firmly settled in the soul, and not yet actually encountered. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 41, verse 51–54:

(p-495) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself, and when evil touches him, he is one of lengthy supplication.﴾ ﴿Say: "Have you considered? If it is from Allah and you have disbelieved in it, who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?"﴾ ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth. Is it not sufficient that your Lord is over all things a witness?﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord. Unquestionably, He is encompassing of all things.﴾

Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the blameworthy character traits of man in general. These are clearly and firmly established among the disbelievers. As for the believer, in most cases he gives thanks when blessed, and he often shows patience in hardship.

The majority of the reciters and the people read ﴿"wa-na'a"﴾ with the hamza as the 'ayn of the verb (nā'a). Ibn 'Amir read "wa-nā'in" with the hamza as the lam of the verb (nā'a), and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far. The meaning in both is one. Abu 'Ali said: nā'a is the inversion of na'ā, "it returned, fa'ala, fala'a" (a morphological pattern). From it is the saying of the poet:

"Every friend who saw me, he says,
'Because of you, this is the head (of grief) of today or tomorrow.'"

And from it is the saying of another:

"And the people of the race have made me something to be looked at, and they have gone to extremes..."

(p-496) And "nā'a" means: he distanced himself and did not incline toward gratitude or obedience.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so he is one of lengthy supplication﴾, that is, "long" as well. He dispensed with one attribute in place of its necessary companion, since "wide" (ʿarīḍ) implies and includes "long" (ṭawīl). He did not say "ṭawīl" because the long may not be wide, so ʿarīḍ is more indicative of abundance.

Then Allah commanded His Prophet, upon him blessings and peace, to present this argument to the Quraysh and the point of their self-deception, so He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: "Have you considered? If this law is from Allah and by His command, and you oppose it, are you not in ruin from Allah, Exalted is He? So who is more astray than one who remains in such deception with Allah, Exalted is He?"﴾ And this is the opposition.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, promised His Prophet ﷺ that He would show the disbelievers His signs. The interpreters differed regarding the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in the horizons and within themselves﴾. Al-Minhal, as-Suddi, and a group said: it is a promise of what Allah, Exalted is He, would open for His Messenger ﷺ of the regions around Makkah and other lands such as Khaybar and the like, and "within themselves" he intended the conquest of Makkah.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a good interpretation that encompasses the announcement of an unseen matter that would appear and be proved afterward, and the wording of the future tense in the verb fits with it. Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah said: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾ is what befell the nations that denied in the regions of the earth in former times, and ﴿and within themselves﴾ is the Day of Badr. Ibn Zayd and 'Ata' said: ﴿"the horizons"﴾ are the horizons of the sky, and he intended by it the signs in the sun, the moon, the winds, and other things. And ﴿"within themselves"﴾ is man's lesson from his body, his senses, his wondrous creation, and his development in the womb, and the like.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These are signs that have been established in a fixed order, so this meaning does not fit with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"We will show them"﴾. The first interpretation is the most preferable of them, and Allah knows best.

(p-497) The pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that it is the truth﴾ refers to the law and the Qur'an. Thus, by Allah's manifesting it and opening lands upon it, it became clear to them that it is the truth. Then He, Exalted is He, said as a promise to His Prophet, upon him blessings and peace: ﴿Is it not sufficient that your Lord...﴾ and the estimate is: "Is it not sufficient that your Lord...?" The bāʾ is extra for emphasis. The "an" may be in the nominative position as a substitution for the place (of the subject), since the estimate is: "Is it not sufficient that your Lord?" It may also be in the genitive position as a substitution for the wording, and all of this is substitution of inclusion. It is also valid that it be in the accusative position by dropping the preposition, meaning: "because He." Al-Jumhur read ﴿"[annahu]"﴾ with a fatḥa on the alif, and some people read ﴿[innahu]﴾ with a kasra, as a parenthetical interjection in the midst of speech.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿[alā]﴾ is an opening that requires the listener's attention to what is said to him. So He began the announcement that they are in doubt, suspicion, and error, which led them to doubt the resurrection. The majority of people read ﴿"fī mirya"﴾ with a kasra on the mīm, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and al-Hasan read [fī murya] with a ḍamma on the mīm, and the meaning is one. Then He began the announcement of His encompassing of all things, in the sense of a warning to them. His encompassing, Exalted is He, is by power and authority. There is no god but Him, the Mighty, the Wise.

The commentary of Surah Ḥā Mīm as-Sajdah is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

"Every friend who saw me, he says,

And from it is the saying of another:
